summary: Describes how to map between SIP and ISUP, the ISDN User Part of SS7, so that SIP calls can interwork with the public telephone network. It is intended for environments where part of a call goes through the PSTN.

plainLanguage.summary: The old phone network and internet calls use different ways to start a call. This document is a translation guide between them.

questions: how does isup map to sip
how do sip calls interwork with the pstn
what is a media gateway controller
how do isdn cause codes map to sip status codes
how does a sip call connect to the pstn
subtitle: How a gateway translates calls between SIP and ISUP so internet telephony can reach the phone network and back.

tldr.problem: Telephone calls on the PSTN are controlled by ISUP signaling over SS7, while SIP is used on IP networks, so calls crossing between the two need a defined translation.
tldr.mechanism: A Media Gateway Controller runs a state machine for each direction, mapping ISUP messages such as IAM, ACM and ANM to SIP INVITE and responses, ISUP parameters to SIP headers, and ISDN cause codes to SIP status codes.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends functionally equivalent call flows, with deviations allowed for national ISUP variants, and it warns that gateways should not blindly trust ISUP carried inside SIP.

today: RFC 3398 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is aimed at gateways between SIP and ISUP networks and stays focused on calls rather than on trunk maintenance.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
SIP sets up, ends and changes multimedia sessions, and a phone call is just a session with audio. ISUP, the ISDN User Part, is a protocol in SS7 networks that controls telephone calls and maintains the network, for example by blocking or resetting circuits.

A module that converts between them is usually called a Media Gateway Controller (MGC), also called a softswitch or call agent. It often controls a Media Gateway (MG) that connects E1/T1 trunks on the PSTN side to IP interfaces. The RFC describes logic an MGC might use, matching messages and parameters, plus how two parallel state machines stay in step.

The scope is deliberately narrow. Only ISUP call functionality is covered, and SIP gets a mapping only for parameters that proxies might use for routing, such as the called party number. ITU-T ISUP is used throughout, with some ANSI and TTC differences noted. Overlap dialing with the Subsequent Address Message is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone companies and internet-calling use different languages to start a call. A translator box sits between them, and this document says how the translator should work.

sections.title: Scenarios and SIP Bridging
sections.content:
In the simple scenario one MGC sits between a PSTN switch and a SIP user agent, and generates the messages for each side using the methods in the RFC.

In SIP bridging a call starts in the PSTN, crosses a SIP network and ends in the PSTN again. To keep the call transparent between the two switches, the ingress MGC places the incoming ISUP message in the body of the SIP message, using the encoding defined in RFC 3204. The egress MGC then uses that encapsulated ISUP, possibly adjusted, for example after SIP redirection. If the recipient does not understand the ISUP body, a negotiation with the SIP Accept and Require headers takes place and later messages leave it out.

A Signaling Gateway may sit between the PSTN and the MGC, but the mapping does not depend on how ISUP is transported. A gateway MUST wait for a complete ISUP message, including any following Segmentation Message, before it sends an INVITE.
sections.plainLanguage: When a call goes phone to internet to phone, the first translator tucks the original phone message in an envelope so the last translator can read it as written.

sections.title: SIP Features the Mapping Relies On
sections.content:
Base SIP is not enough; several extra mechanisms are needed. Without them a call can still proceed, but behavior may differ from what the user expects, for example the other party may answer before the caller hears ringback.

  • Encapsulation: SIP must carry ISUP payloads gateway to gateway; user agents that do not understand ISUP may ignore them.
  • Multipart bodies: PSTN interworking nodes MUST understand multipart/mixed, since a message may hold both SDP and ISUP.
  • Reliable provisional responses: 1xx responses carry call progress and MUST be sent reliably end to end.
  • INFO method: gateways MUST support INFO for mid-call events that match no SIP method, and MUST treat 405 and 501 answers to INFO as non-fatal.
  • DTMF: tones may be carried in band as in RFC 2833.

The RFC also discusses early media, privacy for presentation-restricted callers, and CANCEL, which cannot carry a body, so a non-normal ISUP cause cannot travel in it. Gateways MAY use extra mechanisms, such as the Reason header in RFC 3326, for the cause.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain SIP is like a basic walkie-talkie. To translate phone calls well, it needs a few extra buttons, like a way to send notes along and to say when ringing starts.

sections.title: From SIP to ISUP
sections.content:
When an INVITE arrives the gateway MAY send 100 Trying, MUST reserve media resources (typically an E1/T1 time slot and an RTP/UDP port), then sends an IAM (Initial Address Message) and starts timer T7, whose default is 20 to 30 seconds. Every IAM MUST contain five mandatory parameters: Called Party Number, Nature of Connection Indicators, Forward Call Indicators, Calling Party's Category, and a bearer parameter (Transmission Medium Requirement or User Service Information). Values that SIP cannot supply must be provisioned as defaults.

SIP header values overwrite any encapsulated ISUP values. For example, if the Request-URI says tel:+15105550110 but the encapsulated IAM has another number, the Request-URI wins. If the Request-URI and To header differ, the To header SHOULD fill the Original Called Number.

Responses map back as follows: an ACM generally becomes a 18x response (180 Ringing when the backward indicators say subscriber free), a CPG becomes 180, 181 or 183 by event code, and an ANM or CON becomes 200 OK. If T7 expires, the gateway SHOULD send 504 to SIP and a REL with cause 102 to the PSTN.

For call end, a BYE yields a 200 and a REL with cause 16 (normal clearing), answered by RLC. A CANCEL before a final response gets 200, then 487, and also a REL with cause 16.
sections.plainLanguage: When an internet caller dials, the translator tells the phone network the number, waits for it to say ringing and then answered, and tells the caller each step.

sections.title: From ISUP to SIP
sections.content:
When an IAM arrives, the gateway builds an INVITE. The called number, converted by the rules for telephony URIs, goes into the Request-URI and normally the To header, unless an Original Called Number makes the To differ. The From header takes the calling party number, or a dummy SIP URI naming only the gateway when there is none. A 100 response triggers no ISUP message.

Provisional answers become ISUP messages: 180 Ringing becomes an ACM with subscriber free, 181 an early ACM plus a CPG with event 6, and 182 or 183 an ACM with no indication, or a CPG if an ACM was already sent. A 200 OK becomes an ANM (a CON if no ACM was sent yet, in variants that have CON) and an ACK. A 3xx redirect lets the gateway try the Contact URIs, perhaps with a new IAM. A 4xx to 6xx failure leads to a REL.

A gateway MAY use timer T11 to send an early ACM and so stop the remote node's T7 from expiring while SIP is slow to answer. If the PSTN side hangs up before an answer, the gateway MUST send CANCEL. A caller hanging up during a call leads to a BYE. Suspend and Resume messages MAY be mapped to re-INVITEs or INFO requests, and a re-INVITE that puts the call on hold SHOULD produce a CPG. Reset and hardware blocking messages release calls, and a failed continuity check means no INVITE MUST be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: When a phone caller dials in, the translator asks the internet side, passes along its ringing and answer news as phone signals, and hangs up both sides in the right order.

sections.title: Mapping Failure Codes
sections.content:
ISUP ends or rejects calls with a REL carrying an ISDN cause code, while SIP uses BYE, CANCEL and status codes. The RFC gives RECOMMENDED tables for both directions. If a REL arrives with a cause not in the table, the default is 500 Server internal error. In the other direction, an unlisted SIP status maps to cause 31 (normal, unspecified).

Some causes have no SIP equivalent. Cause 44 (requested circuit not available) means the originating switch should retry with a different circuit, which is internal to the gateway, so no SIP status is sent. If a REL carries cause 22 with a new number in its diagnostic, the gateway SHOULD return 301 with a Contact header.

Where a SIP rejection contains an encapsulated REL, its cause value SHOULD be reused. Otherwise 6xx codes get location 'user' and 4xx and 5xx get 'network'. Some SIP errors, marked in the table, should first be fixed by retrying rather than failing the ISUP half of the call, and a gateway that can authenticate after 401 or 407 SHOULD do so.
sections.plainLanguage: When a call fails, each side has its own way of saying why. The translator has a dictionary that turns 'line busy' into the right code on the other side.

sections.title: Telephone Numbers in URIs
sections.content:
Numbers appear in SIP either as a tel: URL or as the user part of a SIP URI, such as sip:+17208881000@level3.com. A leading + means a full E.164 number with country code. Without it the number may only be nationally significant, and a SIP URI SHOULD carry ;user=phone. The RFC strongly recommends passing only internationally significant numbers between SIP-T gateways.

ISUP stores a number as a Nature of Address byte, a Numbering Plan Indicator byte and BCD digits; the calling party form adds presentation and screening bits. To go from ISUP to a tel URL, an international number gets tel:+ and the digits unchanged, and a national number must have a country code added. To go the other way, a country code local to the gateway is stripped and the number marked national; otherwise it stays international. The numbering plan MUST be set to the ISDN plan.

If presentation is restricted, the From header SHOULD be Anonymous <sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid>. Screening indicators are not translated. The optional number portability fields use npdi=yes and rn=, and an rn= value MUST NOT start with a plus sign.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone numbers are written differently in each world. The translator rewrites them, adding or removing the country part, so the other side can find the right person.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main risk is trusting ISUP carried inside SIP. Gateways SHOULD NOT blindly trust embedded ISUP unless the request was strongly authenticated and the sender is trusted, such as an authorized MGC. For requests from arbitrary endpoints they SHOULD filter ISUP, accepting only known-safe commands and parameters, since deleting believed-dangerous entries does not work well.

Other risks come from users controlling SIP fields. Users can set number portability fields, the To header (and so the Original Called Number) and the From header, so gateways should authenticate the originator before using the From value as the calling number, and gateways MUST support Digest authentication. Cause codes mapped from SIP responses and early media cut through at an 18x are also noted; the RFC says an implementer MAY cut off early media on a brief timer, and that 20 or 30 seconds should be enough. A malicious user could also tie up gateway ports with simultaneous requests, so gateways MAY limit simultaneous requests per authenticated source.

Privacy needs more than encrypting the ISUP body: if the calling number is mapped openly to the From header, a presentation-restricted caller is still exposed.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator should not believe every envelope it is handed. It checks who sent it and limits what it will accept.
